story_facts: P000411. Philip was Titian's most important patron; they met in Milan and Augsburg when Philip was a prince. X-rays show it is painted over an earlier armoured portrait of his father Charles V. Philip wrote to his aunt that it was 'made with haste'; Titian slimmed and idealised him. (Room confirmed on EN and ES pages: Sala 027 - not 041.)

P000422. One of the poesie painted for Philip II (1553-62), meant to hang together in a camerino. Shows Adonis pulling away from Venus, a moment not in Ovid. Contemporaries thought it the most erotic of the series; a Spanish ambassador called it too lascivious.

P000440. Replacement for a 1557 Entombment lost in transit to Philip II. The Virgin holds Christ's limp arm, a detail from Aretino not the Gospels. X-rays show Nicodemus first wore a turban and the Magdalen's hand was moved.

P000441. Late version in same room as E22a. Nicodemus may resemble Titian's own 1550 self-portrait engraving (Gentili). Came to the royal collection in 1585 from Antonio Perez's goods; Aranjuez and Escorial before reaching the Prado in 1839.

P000407. Room 041 confirmed. Rare profile self-portrait (profiles mostly used for the dead). Gold chain of a Knight of the Golden Spur plus brush - echoes 'PICTOR ET EQUES'. Probably the portrait Vasari saw in Titian's studio in 1566.

P000147. Painted in London when he was nearly 70 and sent as a gift to Philip IV, delivered by his son Francesco in 1633. Second version: the first (National Gallery London) was for Henrietta Maria at Greenwich. Every figure except baby Moses is female; Miriam offers their mother as wet nurse.

P000201. Room 006 confirmed on EN and ES pages. Commissioned by Cardinal Alessandro Ludovisi 1617-18 (Mahon). One elder gestures for silence toward the viewer, making us voyeurs/accomplices. Susanna's pose draws on the antique Crouching Aphrodite.

P002631. Venus grazed by Cupid's arrow falls for Adonis (Ovid, Met. X). Venetian/Titianesque landscape and light fused with Correggio, Raphael, Michelangelo and antique sculpture. Bought by Philip IV in 1664 from heirs of Genoese Giovanni Francesco Serra.

P003090. Room 026 confirmed. Losing suitors died; Venus gave Hippomenes three golden apples. Reni shows the moment before the third apple is dropped, hidden behind his back. Debate whether Madrid or Naples (Capodimonte) version came first; Pepper favoured Madrid.

Largest of his early Seville works; first recorded at the Jesuit novitiate of San Luis, Seville. Read as a family portrait (Serrera): the white-bearded king may be Pacheco, his father-in-law. Portraits in Adorations have precedent (Botticelli) but Velazquez gives them unusual weight.

official_title: View of the Gardens of the Villa Medici, Rome, with a Statue of Ariadne
story_facts: P001211. Painted during his 1629-30 Italian stay; probably among four small landscapes sold to Philip IV in 1634. Painted from life outdoors, unlike Claude/Poussin studio landscapes. Sleeping Ariadne framed in the central arch.

official_title: View of the Gardens of the Villa Medici, Rome
story_facts: Location field reads '(Temporary Exhibition)', no room - do not route visitors. Facts: likely painted on the spot; no narrative subject - nature for its own sake; dating debated (first vs second Rome trip); pair read as 'midday'/'evening', anticipating Monet.

P001117. Jacob asleep with a ladder of light and angels (Genesis), turned into a resting shepherd in the countryside. Possibly in Jeronimo de la Torre's 1658 inventory; in 1746 in Isabel Farnese's collection it was attributed to Murillo.

P001239. NOTE: no Zurbaran 'Saint Casilda' on the Prado site (only Bayeu/Gonzalez Velazquez drawings); this Zurbaran is now titled Saint Elisabeth of Portugal - page says it was believed to represent Casilda 'until fairly recently'. Aragonese princess, queen of Portugal, later Poor Clare in Coimbra (d.1336). Alms hidden in her robes turned to roses in midwinter. Possibly a Sevillian noblewoman dressed as a saint.

P000962. EN page fetch failed twice; ES page used (Sala 017, Expuesto). Christ Child as Good Shepherd, popular for private devotion in Seville. Classical ruins = Virgilian pastoral + defeated paganism. Canvas enlarged before 1746 to pair with Saint John the Baptist as a Child.

P000996. Eliezer seeks a wife for Isaac and Rebecca offers water at the well - a pretext for an everyday Andalusian square with women filling pitchers. Owned by Isabel Farnese (La Granja 1746, later Aranjuez); entered the Prado 1819.

P001678. Painted for Philip IV's Torre de la Parada hunting lodge. Two small stars beside Saturn may echo Galileo's 1610 view of Saturn's ring as two satellites. Visible corrections (pentimenti) around the right arm and left heel. (Goya's Saturn is separate, Room 067.)

P001549. Jordaens with wife Catharina van Noort, daughter Elizabeth (born June 1617 - dates the picture) and a servant. Garden-of-love tradition (Rubens, later Watteau). Symbols: parrot = fidelity, dog = loyalty, Cupid fountain = love, lute = harmony.

official_title: The Archduke Leopold William in his Picture Gallery in Brussels
story_facts: P001813. A visual inventory of a real collection, mostly Italian pictures. One of several versions sent as diplomatic gifts; this one went to Philip IV, perhaps to show Brussels rivalled Madrid. Includes Gossaert's St Luke, Van Dyck's Isabella Clara Eugenia, and Raphael's St Margaret.

P001731. Room 078 confirmed (early version). Paris holds the golden apple, eyes on Venus; Minerva's weapons in the foreground. Shaped by Rubens's Italian years and classical sculpture. First recorded in Madrid's Alcazar in 1666.
